newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia said interested in gene-altered soybeans.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia said interested in gene-altered soybeans.

text.p: Indonesia may buy genetically altered soybeans while other Asian buyers shrugged off the controversy the beans have drawn in Europe, traders and officials said on Friday.
Their acceptance in Indonesia, the world's fourth most populous nation with nearly 200 million people, could be less difficult than in Europe due to a lack of consumer awareness.

A senior official of the environmental group Walhi in Indonesia said she was "not familiar yet" with genetically modified U.S. soybeans produced by Monsanto Co and the vehement protests led by Greenpeace to keep them out of Europe.

"I don't think there will be much of an impact here," one senior trader in Jakarta said. "People here don't really talk about it. I just don't have the feeling there is much concern, awareness or knowledge about this affair."
"But of course if it gets blown up, there might be some spillover here," he added. "At the moment, there's nothing."
Soybeans are an important source of protein for Indonesians who cannot afford to eat meat regularly and is also used as a component in making feedmeal for the livestock industry.
Another trader said Indonesia could be a potential export market for the hybrid soybeans if their nutritional value was similar to natural species and prices were lower.

"That is a possibility at this moment," he said, adding that the final decision would, however, depend on how the controversy is resolved in Europe. Indonesia is the biggest importer of grains and oilseeds in Southeast Asia.
The reaction of other major consumers in Asia was muted.
South Korea was little concerned with the U.S. soybeans since it has not yet begun importing the beans, government officials and industry traders said.
"We haven't imported the controversial gene-altered U.S. soybeans this year," an official at Seoul's Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry said.
South Korea's soybean imports this year is expected to total 1.2 million tonnes, the ministry official said.

Traders in the local soybean crushing industry said even if the altered soybeans were imported, it would be difficult to find out how much gene-altered soybean was being imported because the altered soybeans would be mixed in with conventional ones.
"We have been informed by our suppliers that the soybean has been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration," said a senior official with a leading Korean soybean crusher.
"We have not heard of any evidence of problems caused by the gene-altered soybeans," said an official with state-run Korea Consumer Protection Board.
An official with the environmental group Green Korea said they didn't have much information on the U.S. soybeans but were trying to collect more.
But in general, Green Korea, the country's largest environmental group, opposes any move to use artificially altered genes for agricultural products.
Seoul-based foreign traders said they had already informed their clients of the possibility of shipments of the gene-altered U.S. soybeans.

"We have informed our clients (in) Shindongbang Corp, Cheiljedang Corp and Sam Yang Foods Co Ltd, of the gene-altered U.S. soybean. But we have not heard anything," said a Seoul-based Japanese soybean trader.
He said Tokyo has already allowed imports of the soybean.
"In Japan, some consumers are making a little noise but it was not serious," he said.

"The gene-altered U.S. soybeans may be shipped to South Korea from December. If South Korean buyers insist on buying conventional soybeans, they may be asked to pay $40 to $50 per tonne more than normal cost," he said.
Taiwan soybean buyers said they consider genetically altered U.S. soybean to be safe, but said they would press the government to confirm this belief.

"We will ask the government to conduct tests or to acquire U.S. and Japan's research reports to confirm the safety of the genetically altered soybeans," a leading Taiwan soybean buyer, Chen Fa-chen, told Reuters by telephone.
Chen said the controversial soybeans should be safe.
"We have good faith in the U.S. government's safety standards and a confirmation from Japan further assured us of the safety of the modified soybeans," he said.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
